title: Marburg virus persistence and clinical complications among recovered persons in Rwanda: a longitudinal study protocol.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the limited knowledge of Marburg virus (MARV) persistence, long-term clinical outcomes among recovered persons, and protective immunity, given the potential threat to global health security and the scarcity of systematic approaches in African settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A longitudinal study protocol was developed to investigate MARV persistence in body fluids of recovered persons, characterise associated clinical complications, identify factors associated with viral persistence, classify the protective immune response, and discover genomic variants during viral persistence in Rwanda.
analysis.methods: The study will enrol individuals who survived Marburg virus disease (MVD), individuals with natural antibodies for MARV, close contacts, and low-risk controls. Participants will undergo serial sampling of blood, urine, semen, and other relevant specimens over 24 months post-recovery, with continuous clinical assessments and laboratory analyses including molecular detection, serological profiling, immunological assays, and genomic viral characterisation.
analysis.main_results: The study aims to generate critical evidence on MARV persistence, clinical sequelae, and risk factors, which will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conferences, and policy briefs targeting national and global stakeholders.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings will inform survivor care guidelines, transmission mitigation strategies, and future outbreak preparedness, contributing novel insights into the persistence and clinical outcomes of MARV infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study will provide essential evidence to improve survivor care, mitigate transmission risks, and enhance preparedness for future outbreaks, with implications for surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment of Marburg virus disease.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the potential for selection bias due to enrolment of survivors and close contacts, and the generalisability may be limited to the Rwandan context. The evidence strength is moderate due to the prospective cohort design and comprehensive sampling and analysis protocols.

analysis.summary_en: This longitudinal study protocol aims to investigate Marburg virus persistence and clinical outcomes among recovered persons in Rwanda, addressing gaps in knowledge and informing survivor care and outbreak preparedness.

title: Strengthening diagnostic capacity for viral hemorrhagic fevers in Forest Guinea: advances in Lassa fever case detection

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to strengthen diagnostic capacity for viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) in resource-limited settings, addressing gaps exposed by the 2014-2016 Ebola epidemic in Guinea.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A decentralized diagnostics laboratory strengthening program was implemented in Guéckédou and N'Zérékoré, Guinea, from 2017 to 2024, testing 4683 samples from suspected VHF cases.
analysis.methods: Samples were tested using molecular methods, identifying 47 positive cases, including Lassa fever and Ebola virus disease, with a case fatality rate of 67.9%.
analysis.main_results: Of the 4683 samples, 47 (1%) were positive for VHFs, including 30 Lassa fever cases, with a case fatality rate of 67.9%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study confirmed the importance of locally embedded laboratory capacity in enhancing VHFs preparedness, surveillance, and response in Guinea, supporting Lassa fever epidemiology and health-system resilience.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for sustained investment in laboratory capacity to improve early detection and rapid response to VHF outbreaks in resource-limited settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the potential for sampling bias and the need for larger sample sizes to generalize findings, assessed as moderate evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study strengthened diagnostic capacity for viral hemorrhagic fevers in Guinea, identifying 47 positive cases, including 30 Lassa fever cases, and confirming the importance of locally embedded laboratory capacity in preparedness and response.
